work: Enarratio in Epistolam catholicam B. Jacobi
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: PROSECUTIO ELUCIDATIONIS HUJUS CAPITULI PRIMI, AB EO LOCO : BEATUS VIR, ETC.
1.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of this first chapter, from the place: Blessed is the man, etc.

paras.t: CONSEQUENTER sanctus apostolus Jacobus docet tribulationes vitæ præsentis æquanimiter sustinendas, propter earum perpetuam remunerationem. Beatus vir, id est, felix homo est jam in spe et in merito, qui suffert tentationem, id est, impugnationem, tribulationem, afflictionem, sive ab invisibili, sive a visibili hoste inflictam, aut ex fomite seu sensualitatis infectione exortam, æquanimiter tolerat, eamque superat, non ruendo ad impatientiam, iniquum consensum, aut aliam culpam. Et præsertim beatus est, qui pro fide atque justitia persecutionem patitur, nec superatur. Quoniam quum probatus fuerit, id est per adversitatum et impugnationum victoriam approbatus, et Deo acceptus factus, seu sufficienter examinatus et expurgatus, accipiet coronam vitæ, id est præmium essentiale, quod aurea appellatur; præmium quoque accidentale ac speciale, in signum præmiumque victoriæ, quod nuncupatur aureola, si pro justitia pertulerit mortem. De hac corona fertur in Psalmo : Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso. Denique istud est quod spopondit Christus : Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ. Sic ergo omnipotens Deus, quos ad modicum tempus probat, affligit, exercet, in æternum copiose remunerat. Propter quod in Sapientiæ libro dicitur : In paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur : quoniam Deus tentavit illos, et invenit illos dignos se. Hinc sanctus Job : Probavit me, inquit, tanquam aurum quod per ignem transit. Et Tobiæ angelus dixit : Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te.
paras.en: Next the holy apostle James teaches that the tribulations of the present life are to be borne with an even mind, because of their everlasting reward. [[1:12|Blessed is the man|Beatus vir]], that is, a happy man is he already in hope and in merit, [[1:12|that endureth temptation|qui suffert tentationem]], that is, who bears with an even mind assault, tribulation and affliction, whether inflicted by the invisible or by a visible enemy, or arising from the fomes [the tinder of sin left in fallen nature] or the infection of sensuality, and overcomes it, not falling into impatience, wicked consent or any other fault. And above all blessed is he who suffers persecution for faith and justice[[Matt 5:10||]] and is not overcome. [[1:12|for, when he hath been proved|Quoniam quum probatus fuerit]], that is, approved through victory over adversities and assaults, and made acceptable to God, or sufficiently examined and purged, [[1:12|he shall receive the crown of life|accipiet coronam vitæ]], that is, the essential reward, which is called the aurea; and also the accidental and special reward, as sign and prize of victory, which is called the aureola, if he has endured death for justice. Of this crown it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 20:4|thou hast set on his head a crown of precious stones|Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso]]. And this is what Christ promised: [[Apoc 2:10|Be thou faithful unto death: and I will give thee the crown of life|Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ]]. Thus almighty God rewards abundantly for ever those whom for a little while He proves, afflicts and exercises. Hence it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:5|Afflicted in few things, in many they shall be well rewarded: because God hath tried them, and found them worthy of himself|In paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur : quoniam Deus tentavit illos, et invenit illos dignos se]]. Hence holy Job says: [[Job 23:10|and has tried me as gold that passeth through the fire|Probavit me, inquit, tanquam aurum quod per ignem transit]]. And the angel said to Tobias: [[Tob 12:13|because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee|Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te]].

paras.t: Accipiet ergo post vitam præsentem, quum fuerit plene purgatus, coronam vitæ, quam repromisit Deus diligentibus se : quia per angelos sanctos, per Apostolos et Prophetas promisit hoc. Imo Christus Dei Filius, Deus vere incarnatus, proprio ore eam promisit in Evangelio palam ac sæpe. Porro per hoc quod ait, Quam repromisit Deus diligentibus se, duo innuuntur. Primum est, quod nulla actio nullaque passio, sine caritate sit meritoria. Tentationes autem et tribulationes meritoriæ sunt vitæ æternæ, in quantum ex caritate æquanimiter tolerantur, acceptantur, atque vincuntur. Ideo ait Apostolus : Si tradidero corpus meum ita ut ardeam, caritatem autem non habuero, nihil mihi prodest. Secundum est, quod Deus his quos amplius diligit, frequenter plures et graviores tribulationes immittit. Idcirco in adversis et tentationibus nequaquam frangamur, nec pusillanimes efficiamur, nec fatigemur animis nostris : imo eas tanquam probabile argumentum divinæ dilectionis ad nos, suscipiamus ac superemus ; correptiones et correctiones amemus, illud Judith pensantes : Memores esse debemus quomodo pater noster Abraham tentatus est, et per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est. Sic Isaac, sic Jacob, sic Moyses, et omnes qui placuerunt Deo, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles. Qui autem tentationes non susceperunt in timore Domini, in impatientia sua exterminati sunt.
paras.en: So after the present life, when he has been fully purged, he shall receive the crown of life, [[1:12|which God hath promised to them that love him|quam repromisit Deus diligentibus se]]: for He promised this through the holy angels, through the Apostles and Prophets. Nay, Christ the Son of God, God truly incarnate, promised it with His own mouth in the Gospel, openly and often[[Matt 5:10||]]. Now by his saying, Which God hath promised to them that love him, two things are hinted. The first is that no action and no suffering is meritorious without charity. Temptations and tribulations are meritorious of eternal life in so far as they are borne, accepted and overcome with an even mind out of charity. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 13:3|if I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing|Si tradidero corpus meum ita ut ardeam, caritatem autem non habuero, nihil mihi prodest]]. The second is that God often sends more and heavier tribulations to those whom He loves more. Therefore let us by no means be broken in adversities and temptations, nor become faint-hearted, nor grow weary in our minds; rather let us receive and overcome them as a credible proof of God's love towards us; let us love reproofs and corrections, weighing that word of Judith: They must remember [[Jdt 8:22|how our father Abraham was tempted, and being proved by many tribulations, was made the friend of God|quomodo pater noster Abraham tentatus est, et per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est]]. [[Jdt 8:23|So Isaac, so Jacob, so Moses, and all that have pleased God, passed through many tribulations, remaining faithful|Sic Isaac, sic Jacob, sic Moyses, et omnes qui placuerunt Deo, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles]]. But those who did not receive temptations in the fear of the Lord were destroyed in their impatience[[Jdt 8:24||]].

paras.t: Nemo quum tentatur, dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur. Postquam apostolus Jacobus locutus est de tentationibus quas exterius causa probationis patimur, nunc agit de tentationibus quas intus, suadente diabolo, aut infectione naturæ nostræ movente, causa deceptionis toleramus. Unde Beda hic ait : Duplex est genus tentationis : unum, quod decipit ; aliud, quod probat. Loquendo de tentatione quæ decipit seu intentione fallendi inducitur, Deus neminem tentat. Sed loquendo de tentatione quæ probat, tentavit Abraham Deus. De qua et ait Propheta : Proba me, Domine, et tenta me. Denique, secundum Albertum, per verba prætacta apostolus Jacobus removet quamdam dubitationem. Dixit enim superius in tentationibus esse gaudendum. Ex quo aliquis posset opinari, universas tentationes nobis immitti a Deo. Quod non est verum : quia, secundum Glossam, exteriorem tentationem immittit Deus ad suorum probationem fidelium ; interiorem vero, qua concupiscitur quod lege divina prohibetur, Deus non immittit. Porro, secundum Bedam, per verba jam tacta Jacobus illorum destruit errorem, qui sicut bonas tentationes, ita et malas dixerunt nobis divinitus inspirari. Est autem, secundum Glossam, duplex tentatio : Una exterior, sicut paupertas, infirmitas, incarceratio, et alia quævis exterior tribulatio : cujus Deus non est solum permissor, sed etiam auctor. Tales namque afflictiones sæpe immittit fidelibus pro bono eorum. Alia est tentatio interior, ut prava suggestio, prava cogitatio, qua furtum seu aliud peccatum concipitur : cujus Deus permissor est, non immissor seu actor.
paras.en: [[1:13|Let no man, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God|Nemo quum tentatur, dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur]]. After the apostle James has spoken of the temptations we suffer outwardly for the sake of proving, he now treats of the temptations we endure within, at the devil's persuasion or at the stirring of our nature's infection, for the sake of deceiving. Hence Bede says here: There are two kinds of temptation: one that deceives, another that proves. Speaking of the temptation that deceives, or is brought on with the intention of misleading, God tempts no one. But speaking of the temptation that proves, [[Gen 22:1|God tempted Abraham|tentavit Abraham Deus]]. Of which the Prophet also says: [[Ps 25:2|Prove me, O Lord, and try me|Proba me, Domine, et tenta me]]. Further, according to Albert, by the words just cited the apostle James removes a certain doubt. For he said above that we should rejoice in temptations; from which someone might suppose that all temptations are sent upon us by God. Which is not true: for, according to the Gloss, outward temptation God sends for the proving of His faithful; but inward temptation, by which one covets what the divine law forbids, God does not send. Again, according to Bede, by the words now cited James destroys the error of those who said that as good temptations, so also evil ones are inspired in us by God. Now, according to the Gloss, temptation is twofold: one outward, such as poverty, sickness, imprisonment and any other outward tribulation, of which God is not only the permitter but also the author; for He often sends such afflictions upon the faithful for their good. The other is inward temptation, such as a wicked suggestion or a wicked thought by which theft or some other sin is conceived; of this God is the permitter, not the sender or doer.

paras.t: Pro clariori hujus textus intelligentia quæritur, cujus sit tentare, an scilicet a solo tentemur diabolo, an etiam tentet nos Deus. Et videtur, quod tentemur a Deo, juxta illud : Tentavit Deus Abraham. In Deuteronomio quoque habetur : Recordaberis cuncti itineris, per quod adduxit te Dominus Deus tuus, ut affligeret te atque tentaret. Et Sapiens : Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se. Atque apud Joannem : Hoc dixit Jesus, tentans eum, puta Philippum. In oppositum est auctoritas Jacobi in præsenti. Præterea, super illud Pauli, Ne forte tentet vos is qui tentat, dicit Glossa : Id est diabolus, cujus solius officium est tentare.
paras.en: For a clearer understanding of this text it is asked whose part it is to tempt: that is, whether we are tempted by the devil alone, or whether God also tempts us. And it seems that we are tempted by God, according to that: [[Gen 22:1|God tempted Abraham|Tentavit Deus Abraham]]. In Deuteronomy too we have: [[Deut 8:2|thou shalt remember all the way through which the Lord thy God hath brought thee for forty years through the desert, to afflict thee and to prove thee|Recordaberis cuncti itineris, per quod adduxit te Dominus Deus tuus, ut affligeret te atque tentaret]]. And the Wise Man: [[Wis 3:5|God hath tried them, and found them worthy of himself|Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se]] [Denis has *the just* for *them*]. And in John: [[John 6:6|this he said to try him|Hoc dixit Jesus, tentans eum]], namely Philip. Against this is the authority of James in the present place. Moreover, on that word of Paul, [[1 Thess 3:5|lest perhaps he that tempteth should have tempted you|Ne forte tentet vos is qui tentat]], the Gloss says: That is, the devil, whose office alone it is to tempt.

paras.t: Ad istud Thomas super secundum Sententiarum respondet : Ad perfectam rationem tentationis tria concurrunt. Primum est, ut per tentationem alicujus dubii accipiatur cognitio ; secundum, ut hoc sit a tentante intentum ; tertium, ut ipsemet tentans, cognitionem illius rei accipere velit : et isto modo Deus non tentat, sed homo tentatur ab homine, et etiam a diabolo. Dicitur autem Deus tentare, quantum ad duo prima : ut scilicet alicujus ignoti cognitio manifestetur, non sibi, sed aliis : quod et Deus intendit, ut patuit in tentatione Abrahæ, quem Deus tentavit ut ejus fides et obedientia aliis, ad eorum ædificationem, insinuarentur. Mundus vero et caro dicuntur tentare, solum quantum ad primum trium illorum, ad perfectam tentationis rationem concurrentium : quia ex impugnatione carnis et mundi, manifestatur virtus aut imperfectio mentis, quamvis nec mundus, nec caro intendant hoc. Ipsa ergo impugnatio animæ, seu ejus virtutis, tentatio dicitur. Hæc autem impugnatio, vel est a principio intrinseco, puta a carnis corruptione, et hæc vocatur tentatio carnis ; vel a principio extrinseco, et hoc dupliciter : quia illud extrinsecum, aut impugnat per modum objecti, et sic est tentatio a mundo, cujus rebus corda hominum ad peccandum alliciuntur ; vel per modum agentis ipsum trahit ad peccandum, persuadendo, terrendo, aut blandiendo : et sic est tentatio a diabolo et a membris ipsius. — Dicitur autem diabolus solus tentare, non quod ipse semper sit immediatus tentator, sed quia primo tentavit hominem, ex qua tentatione consecutæ sunt aliæ tentationes. (Tamen, ut asserit Origenes, quamvis non esset diabolus, adhuc homines tentarentur concupiscentia venereorum et alimentorum.) Vel dicitur diabolus solus tentare, quoniam ei et membris suis dumtaxat convenit tentare cum intentione trahendi ad vitium, vel quia utitur carne et rebus mundi tanquam instrumentis ad tentandum hominem.
paras.en: To this Thomas, on the second book of the Sentences, answers: Three things concur in the complete notion of temptation. The first, that through the temptation knowledge of something doubtful is obtained; the second, that this be intended by the tempter; the third, that the tempter himself wishes to obtain knowledge of that thing. In this way God does not tempt, but man is tempted by man, and also by the devil. God is said to tempt as regards the first two: namely, that knowledge of something unknown is made manifest, not to Himself but to others; which God also intends, as appeared in the temptation of Abraham, whom God tempted so that his faith and obedience might be made known to others for their edification[[Gen 22:12||]]. The world and the flesh are said to tempt only as regards the first of those three things that concur in the complete notion of temptation: for through the assault of the flesh and the world the virtue or imperfection of the mind is made manifest, although neither the world nor the flesh intends this. The very assault upon the soul, then, or upon its virtue, is called temptation. Now this assault is either from an intrinsic principle, namely from the corruption of the flesh, and this is called temptation of the flesh; or from an extrinsic principle, and this in two ways: for that extrinsic thing either assails after the manner of an object, and so there is temptation from the world, by whose things the hearts of men are enticed to sin; or after the manner of an agent it draws a man to sin, by persuading, terrifying or flattering, and so there is temptation from the devil and from his members. — The devil is said alone to tempt, not because he is always the immediate tempter, but because he first tempted man, and from that temptation other temptations followed. (Yet, as Origen asserts, even if there were no devil, men would still be tempted by the desire of venereal things and of food.) Or the devil is said alone to tempt, because to him and his members only does it belong to tempt with the intention of drawing to vice; or because he uses the flesh and the things of the world as instruments for tempting man.

paras.t: Insuper, in prima parte Summæ suæ loquitur Thomas : Tentare, est proprie experimentum de aliquo sumere, ut scilicet aliquid circa ipsum, vel de se ipso sciatur. Ideo proximus finis tentantis est cognitio. Ex cognitione autem potest ulterius alius finis intendi, aut bonus, aut malus. Diabolus vero talem cognitionem semper refert ad malum, puta ut fallat et noceat. Sicque proprium diabolo est tentare : quia etsi homo sic tentet, hoc tamen facit ut servus diaboli. Dicitur quoque Deus tentare, non ut sciat, sed ut aliquid faciat scire. Mundus autem et caro non nisi instrumentaliter ac materialiter tentant, præbendo occasionem peccandi. Sed homo tentat aliquem, et bene, et male : bene, dum quærit eum cognoscere ut prosit ; male, dum quærit eum cognoscere ut noceat. Verumtamen per tentationem mundi, quandoque intelligitur tentatio quæ infertur a mundanis et pravis hominibus ; quandoque illa quæ infertur (ut tactum est) a rebus sæculi hujus, puta a divitiis atque honoribus ejus.
paras.en: Further, in the first part of his Summa Thomas says: To tempt is properly to make trial of someone, namely so that something may be known about him or about himself. Hence the proximate end of the tempter is knowledge. But from knowledge some further end may be intended, either good or evil. The devil always refers such knowledge to evil, namely to deceive and to harm. And so tempting is proper to the devil: for even if a man tempts in this way, he does it as the devil's servant. God too is said to tempt, not that He may know, but that He may make something known. The world and the flesh tempt only instrumentally and materially, by furnishing occasion of sin. But a man tempts another both well and ill: well, when he seeks to know him in order to help him; ill, when he seeks to know him in order to harm him. Yet by the temptation of the world is sometimes understood the temptation brought by worldly and wicked men; sometimes that brought (as was touched on) by the things of this world, namely by its riches and honours.

paras.t: His præmissis, præsens textus facile intelligetur. Nemo quum tentatur, tentatione interiori ad fallendum tendente et inclinante ad vitium, dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur, ita ut Deus inclinet aut cogat eum ad culpam. Deus enim intentator malorum est, id est, malorum tentamentorum non est suggestor, aut auctor, nec est tentator malorum seu vitiorum, id est tentativa causa eorum ; ipse enim neminem tentat tentatione ad malum ordinata. Sed objici potest, quia tentatio tam activa quam passiva, sunt quidam actus et aliquid positivum : ergo a Deo sunt, a quo omnis entitas derivatur, et in quem omnes effectus, id est actus, tanquam in primum effectivum principium reducuntur. Et respondendum, quod omnis effectus et actus, in quantum est ens et aliquid positivum, a Deo sunt tanquam a prima causa : sed in quantum habent deformitatem et obliquitatem peccati, nihil sunt et sola privatio ; nec habent causam efficientem, sed deficientem, videlicet voluntatem creatam, ut defectivam : quemadmodum claudicatio, in quantum est ambulatio quædam, est a virtute motiva et progressiva ; deformitas autem hujusmodi ambulationis, est a tibiæ indispositione.
paras.en: These things premised, the present text will easily be understood. [[1:13|Let no man, when he is tempted|Nemo quum tentatur]] with the inward temptation that tends to deceive and inclines to vice, [[1:13|say that he is tempted by God|dicat quoniam a Deo tentatur]], as though God inclined or forced him to the fault. [[1:13|For God is not a tempter of evils|Deus enim intentator malorum est]] [the Latin *intentator* means *untempted* or *not a tempter*; Denis takes it in the second sense], that is, He is not the suggester or author of evil temptings, nor the tempter to evils or vices, that is, their tempting cause; [[1:13|and he tempteth no man|ipse enim neminem tentat]] with a temptation directed to evil. But it may be objected that temptation, active as well as passive, is a certain act and something positive; therefore it is from God, from whom all being is derived, and to whom all effects, that is acts, are traced back as to their first efficient principle. And it must be answered that every effect and act, in so far as it is a being and something positive, is from God as from the first cause; but in so far as they have the deformity and crookedness of sin, they are nothing and a mere privation; nor have they an efficient cause, but a deficient one, namely the created will as defective: just as limping, in so far as it is a kind of walking, is from the motive and progressive power, but the deformity of such walking is from the faulty condition of the leg.

paras.t: Unusquisque vero tentatur a concupiscentia sua, id est ab inordinata cupiditate seu privato amore. Nam radix omnium malorum est cupiditas, id est improbus amor sui, pro quo concupiscentia hoc loco accipitur. De quo amore asserit Augustinus, quod sit omnium vitiorum origo, quemadmodum amor Dei est omnis boni principium, omnis scilicet meritorii actus. Unde amor sui crescens usque ad contemptum Dei, civitatem efficit Babylonis, quæ est ecclesia malignantium et regnum diaboli : quemadmodum amor Dei crescens usque ad contemptum sui, constituit civitatem Jerusalem, quæ est Ecclesia Dei viventis et regnum Christi. Ab hac ergo concupiscentia tentatur, id est, radicaliter impugnatur, quicumque tentatur, quia ab ea inclinatur et movetur ad diversa peccata. Non tamen per verba hæc excludit apostolus Jacobus tentationem diaboli, quia frequenter diabolus actuat seu excitat concupiscentiam istam in homine, et per eam tentat eumdem.
paras.en: [[1:14|But every man is tempted by his own concupiscence|Unusquisque vero tentatur a concupiscentia sua]], that is, by inordinate desire or private love. For [[1 Tim 6:10|the desire of money is the root of all evils|radix omnium malorum est cupiditas]] [Latin *cupiditas*, which Denis takes broadly], that is, the wicked love of self, for which concupiscence is taken in this place. Of this love Augustine asserts that it is the origin of all vices, just as the love of God is the beginning of all good, namely of every meritorious act. Hence the love of self growing even to the contempt of God makes the city of Babylon, which is the church of the malignant and the kingdom of the devil; just as the love of God growing even to the contempt of self founds the city of Jerusalem, which is the Church of the living God and the kingdom of Christ. By this concupiscence, then, whoever is tempted is tempted, that is, assailed at the root, for by it he is inclined and moved to various sins. Yet by these words the apostle James does not exclude the temptation of the devil, for the devil often actuates or stirs up this concupiscence in man, and through it tempts him.

paras.t: Tentatur ergo unusquisque a concupiscentia, abstractus, id est a recto salutis itinere et vero rationis judicio, et illectus, id est ad culpam attractus. Deinde concupiscentia quum conceperit, id est, ad consensum perduxerit, parit peccatum, id est, reum facit. Tunc enim est mortale peccatum interius, quum plenus adest consensus de aliquo concupito contra præceptum. Peccatum vero quum consummatum fuerit, id est foris ad effectum perductum, ita quod ex consensu itur in opus, generat mortem, quia inducit ad consuetudinem vitiosam et obstinationem, deinde ad damnationem æternam, quæ est mors secunda gravissima. Unde quod ait, Generat mortem, non est sic intelligendum quasi in solo exteriori opere consistat peccatum mortale, quum in interiori cogitatione et affectione deliberatæ rationis consensum habente, sit culpa mortalis : imo ratio meriti atque demeriti in opere exteriori, dependet ab interiori. Sed ideo dicit sic, quia in opere exteriori magis apparet deformitas vitii, et culpa augetur, ac prava consuetudo incurritur.
paras.en: So every man is tempted by concupiscence, [[1:14|being drawn away|abstractus]], that is, from the right road of salvation and the true judgment of reason, [[1:14|and allured|et illectus]], that is, drawn to the fault. [[1:15|Then, when concupiscence hath conceived|Deinde concupiscentia quum conceperit]], that is, has brought him to consent, [[1:15|it bringeth forth sin|parit peccatum]], that is, makes him guilty. For then there is inward mortal sin, when there is full consent concerning some desired thing against the commandment. [[1:15|But sin, when it is completed|Peccatum vero quum consummatum fuerit]], that is, carried out outwardly into effect, so that from consent one goes on to the deed, [[1:15|begetteth death|generat mortem]], because it leads to vicious habit and obstinacy, and then to eternal damnation, which is the second and most grievous death[[Apoc 21:8||]]. Hence his saying, Begetteth death, is not to be understood as though mortal sin consisted only in the outward deed, since there is mortal guilt in inward thought and affection having the consent of deliberate reason; nay, the character of merit and demerit in the outward deed depends on the inward. But he speaks so because in the outward deed the deformity of vice appears more, the guilt is increased, and wicked habit is incurred.

paras.t: Itaque in verbis præhabitis insinuatur processus humanæ tentationis. Nam primo concupiscentia oritur, per quam incipit homo abstrahi a vero et bono. Deinde concupiscentiæ delectatio quædam conjungitur, per quam homo in malum illicitur. Tunc tamen stat adhuc in terminis peccati venialis. Deinde concupiscentiæ et delectationi consensus deliberatus adjicitur : et tunc est peccatum mortale, ex quo ad opus proceditur, et reiteratio frequens seu consuetudo inde consequitur. Hinc loquitur Beda : Tribus modis tentatio agitur : suggestione, delectatione, consensu : suggestione hostis, delectatione aut etiam consensu nostræ fragilitatis, consensu cordis. Quod si hoste suggerente, nec delectamur nec consentimus, tentatio nobis ad victoriam provenit. Si vero ad hostis suggestionem paulatim a recta intentione abstrahi, atque in vitium incipimus illici delectando, offendimus sed nondum lapsum mortis incurrimus. Quod si peccati in corde concepti delectationem sequatur partus pravæ actionis, aut certe consensus, mortis rei efficimur. Hoc quoque pensandum, quia ut dicunt doctores, non solum plenus consensus in opus, sed et consensus in delectationem prohibitam, est mortalis.
paras.en: Thus in the foregoing words the process of human temptation is indicated. For first concupiscence arises, through which man begins to be drawn away from the true and the good. Then a certain delight is joined to the concupiscence, through which man is allured into evil; yet then he still stands within the bounds of venial sin. Then deliberate consent is added to the concupiscence and the delight, and then there is mortal sin, from which one proceeds to the deed, and frequent repetition, or habit, follows from it. Hence Bede says: Temptation is carried on in three ways: by suggestion, by delight, by consent: by the suggestion of the enemy, by the delight or even the consent of our frailty, by the consent of the heart. If, when the enemy suggests, we neither take delight nor consent, the temptation turns out for our victory. But if at the enemy's suggestion we begin little by little to be drawn away from right intention and to be allured into vice by taking delight, we offend, but do not yet incur the fall of death. But if the delight in sin conceived in the heart is followed by the birth of a wicked action, or certainly by consent, we are made guilty of death. This too is to be weighed: that, as the doctors say, not only full consent to the deed but also consent to forbidden delight is mortal.

paras.t: Nolite itaque errare, fratres mei dilectissimi, per vitiorum abrupta, per errorum ac falsitatum ac perfidiarum obscura (via enim impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt), ne sero pœnitentes, dicatis illud Sapientiæ : Erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis.
paras.en: [[1:16|Do not err, therefore, my dearest brethren|Nolite itaque errare, fratres mei dilectissimi]], over the precipices of vices, through the dark places of errors, falsehoods and perfidies ([[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|via enim impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt]]), lest, repenting too late, you say that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:6|we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis]].

paras.t: (Circa præhabita quæritur, an tentatio sit appetenda. Respondet Albertus : Quædam in sua ratione circumvolutam habent malitiam, ut furtum : quæ nequaquam sunt appetenda. Alia sunt quæ nominata, statim habent circumvolutam bonitatem, ut esse sapientem, et virtute præditum : quæ simpliciter et absque additione sunt appetenda. Alia sunt, quæ de se non sunt appetibilia, quum sint quædam mala pœnalia : tamen per comparationem ad finem sunt appetenda, ut potio amara. Quum ergo tentationes per se ordinentur ab hoste ad hominis deceptionem, per accidens vero ordinentur ad tentati salutem, ex hoc quod Dei gratia auxiliante vincuntur ; idcirco tentari non est simpliciter cupiendum, sed tentari et vincere simul sumptum. Verum quia considerata nostra fragilitate, victoria est incerta, tentatio securius fugitur quam optatur. Et si objiciatur, quia (ut Jacobus ait apostolus) omne gaudium existimare debemus quum in diversas inciderimus tentationes, ergo sunt appetendæ, præsertim quia (ut dictum est) sunt valde multipliciter fructuosæ : respondetur, quod Jacobus loquitur de tentatione tribulationum, ad quarum patientiam exhortatur, quia non nisi per patientiam eas possumus superare. Ideo gaudium et fructuositas non sunt de talibus tribulationibus et tentationibus secundum se, sed magis de patientia, qua vincuntur.
paras.en: (Concerning the foregoing it is asked whether temptation is to be desired. Albert answers: Some things have malice wrapped up in their very notion, such as theft; these are by no means to be desired. Others, as soon as they are named, have goodness wrapped up in them, such as to be wise and endowed with virtue; these are to be desired simply and without qualification. Others are not desirable of themselves, being certain penal evils, yet in relation to an end they are to be desired, like a bitter draught. Since, then, temptations are of themselves directed by the enemy to man's deception, but accidentally are directed to the salvation of the one tempted, because they are overcome with the help of God's grace, therefore to be tempted is not to be desired simply, but to be tempted and to overcome taken together. But since, considering our frailty, victory is uncertain, temptation is more safely fled than wished for. And if it be objected that (as the apostle James says) we ought to count it all joy when we fall into divers temptations[[1:2||]], and that therefore they are to be desired, especially since (as was said) they are fruitful in very many ways: it is answered that James speaks of the temptation of tribulations, to patience in which he exhorts, because only through patience can we overcome them. Therefore the joy and fruitfulness are not of such tribulations and temptations in themselves, but rather of the patience by which they are overcome.

paras.t: Præterea huic rationi concordat responsio Thomæ super secundum Sententiarum, dicentis : Quum bonum sit objectum voluntatis ac desiderii, eo modo aliquid est volendum, quo bonum. Inter bona autem aliquid invenitur quod est bonum simpliciter et per se, sicut sunt bona honesta, puta virtutes : quæ tanquam fines aliorum, sui gratia appetuntur, quamvis in aliud ducant : quia in omnibus honestis utilitas honestati coincidit, nisi in ultimo, quod est finis finium, quod propter se tantum est appetendum. Aliquid vero est, quod in se bonitatem non habet unde appetatur, si absolute consideretur ; sed secundum ordinem ad finem, bonitatem quamdam sortitur, quæ utilitas nominatur : et hæc sunt propter aliud appetenda, ut sectio membri propter sanitatem. Porro ad finem consequendum, contingit aliquid dupliciter ordinari : per se scilicet, et per accidens. Per se dico, quod quantum in se est, in finem debitum est ductivum; per accidens autem, quod quantum in se est, in aliud duceret, sed ex concursu alterius causæ ducit in debitum finem, sicut qui comedit venenum ut moriatur, et contingit ex hoc sanitas. Quum ergo causa per accidens, non sit proportionata ad effectum, sed solum causa per se; idcirco ex ordine ad finem qui est per accidens, non est aliquid bonum aut appetibile, simpliciter acceptum, sed solum concurrentibus omnibus quæ ad hunc finem determinant. Dico igitur, quod tentatio per se, ordinata est ad hominis perditionem; ad salutem vero non ordinatur, nisi per accidens, scilicet ex hoc quod homo eam vincit auxilio gratiæ Dei. Ideo tentari non est simpliciter appetendum, sed tentari et vincere simul acceptum. Sed quoniam propter nostram fragilitatem victoria valde est dubia, securius fugienda est tentatio quam optanda.
paras.en: Moreover, with this reasoning agrees the answer of Thomas on the second book of the Sentences, who says: Since the good is the object of the will and of desire, a thing is to be willed in the way in which it is good. Among goods there is something that is good simply and of itself, as are honest goods [that is, goods of moral worth], namely the virtues: these, as ends of other things, are desired for their own sake, although they lead to something further; for in all honest goods usefulness coincides with honesty, except in the last, which is the end of ends, which is to be desired for its own sake alone. But there is something which has in itself no goodness for which it should be desired, if considered absolutely, but in its ordering to an end obtains a certain goodness which is called usefulness; and these are to be desired for the sake of something else, as the cutting off of a limb for the sake of health. Further, a thing may be ordered to attaining an end in two ways: of itself, and accidentally. Of itself, I say, when of its own nature it leads to the due end; accidentally, when of its own nature it would lead elsewhere, but through the concurrence of another cause leads to the due end, as when someone eats poison in order to die, and health happens to result from it. Since, then, an accidental cause is not proportioned to the effect, but only a cause of itself, therefore from an accidental ordering to an end a thing is not good or desirable taken simply, but only when all the things that determine it to this end concur. I say, therefore, that temptation of itself is ordered to man's perdition; but to salvation it is ordered only accidentally, namely because man overcomes it with the help of God's grace. Therefore to be tempted is not to be desired simply, but to be tempted and to overcome taken together. But since because of our frailty victory is very doubtful, temptation is more safely to be fled than wished for.

paras.t: Insuper istis responsionibus aliquid videtur esse addendum, quia ut tactum est, duplex est genus tentationis : unum quod probat, aliud quod fallit. Quorum primum est a Deo, et ad hominis ordinatur salutem; aliud a diabolo et membris ipsius, ordinaturque ad tentati seductionem. Rursus, sicut præhabitum est, duplex est tentatio, puta exterior, ut est corporalis afflictio, cujus Deus non solum est permissor, sed etiam actor. Est quoque tentatio interior, ad culpam inclinans seu ordinata, cujus Deus permissor est, non immissor. Constat itaque præinductas responsiones non esse prolatas, nisi de tentatione hostis ad fallendum tendente.
paras.en: Further, something seems to need adding to these answers, because, as was touched on, temptation is of two kinds: one that proves, another that deceives. The first of these is from God and is ordered to man's salvation; the other is from the devil and his members, and is ordered to the seduction of the one tempted. Again, as was said before, temptation is twofold: outward, such as bodily affliction, of which God is not only the permitter but also the doer; and inward temptation, inclining or ordered to sin, of which God is the permitter, not the sender. It is clear, then, that the answers brought forward were given only of the enemy's temptation that tends to deceive.

paras.t: Remanet igitur quæstio, an tentatio quæ est ex, vel, a Deo, atque exterior, tendens ad probationem et salutem, sit appetenda. Ad quod respondendum, quod appetenda est eo modo quo medicina amara et afflictiva appetitur propter sanitatem et delectationem. Estque appetenda cum duplici circumspectione. utpote considerata propria fragilitate et defectuositate, ne homo in viribus suis confidat; et præsupposito adjutorio gratiæ Dei, in quo spes tota figatur. Et hoc modo, etiam tentationes hostiles appeti possunt. Verumtamen observandum, quod aliquid est appetibile uni, quod non est appetibile alteri, propter diversam eorum dispositionem. Perfecti ergo et etiam digne proficientes, securius possunt tentationes appetere, cum circumspectionibus memoratis, quam incipientes et imperfecti. Et de hoc in Vitis Patrum multa habentur exempla.
paras.en: There remains, then, the question whether temptation which is from, or by, God, and outward, tending to proving and salvation, is to be desired. To which it must be answered that it is to be desired in the way that a bitter and painful medicine is desired for the sake of health and delight. And it is to be desired with a twofold circumspection: namely, considering one's own frailty and defectiveness, lest a man trust in his own strength; and presupposing the help of God's grace, in which all hope is to be fixed. And in this way even the enemy's temptations can be desired. Yet it is to be observed that something is desirable to one which is not desirable to another, because of their differing disposition. The perfect, then, and also those making worthy progress, can more safely desire temptations, with the circumspections mentioned, than beginners and the imperfect. And of this many examples are found in the Lives of the Fathers.

paras.t: Amplius quæritur, an tentatio quæ est ab hoste, sit peccatum, an etiam tentatio quæ est a mundo, et item an omnis tentatio a carne seu carnis, peccatum sit. Ad hæc Thomas super secundum respondet : Peccatum unius non consistit in actu alterius, sed in proprio actu. Propter quod in Ezechiele legitur : Anima quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur. In tentatione autem carnis, ipse appetitus illicitus, secundum quem tentari quis dicitur, est actus ejus qui tentatur. Non enim sola caro concupiscit, sed conjunctum, videlicet homo. Ideo talis tentatio est peccatum in eo qui tentatur. Siquidem motus concupiscibilis in illicitum tendens, tentatio carnis est. Tentatio autem quæ est a mundo vel ab hoste, est a principio extrinseco : unde actus non pertinet ad tentatum, sed passio tantum. Propter hoc non est peccatum in tali tentatione, nisi per delectationem sive consensum, quia tunc tentatus incipit cooperari tentanti. Præterea, juxta Thomam, diabolus potest imprimere vim imaginativam dupliciter : utpote aliqua sensibilia exterius repræsentando, et ipsam vim imaginativam intus turbando ac alterando. Idcirco, secundum modum quo imprimit in nos, tentare nos dicitur. Hæc tamen impressio non habet rationem peccati, quum non sit in appetitu, sed in apprehensione dumtaxat. Est tamen tendens in culpam, quantum est de intentione tentantis. Hoc quoque pensandum, quia ut Thomas adjungit, motus concupiscibilis potest dupliciter in nobis insurgere : Primo, ex qualitate organi, sicut corpore calefacto, insurgit motus libidinis absque aliqua imaginatione : et iste motus est pure naturalis, nec rationem peccati habens. Et hunc motum potest diabolus ex sua potestate in nobis causare, nisi divina cohibeatur virtute. Secundo, ex apprehensione alicujus delectabilis. Et ex parte illa appetitus habet aliquam libertatem in homine, secundum quod potest obedire imperio rationis : sicque in concupiscibili potest esse peccatum. Sed hunc motum diabolus extorquere non potest.
paras.en: It is further asked whether temptation from the enemy is a sin, and also temptation from the world, and likewise whether every temptation from the flesh, or of the flesh, is a sin. To these Thomas, on the second book, answers: The sin of one does not consist in the act of another, but in one's own act. Hence we read in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:20|The soul that sinneth, the same shall die|Anima quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur]]. Now in the temptation of the flesh, the unlawful appetite itself, according to which one is said to be tempted, is the act of him who is tempted. For it is not the flesh alone that covets, but the composite, namely the man. Therefore such temptation is a sin in him who is tempted; for a movement of the concupiscible power tending to what is unlawful is the temptation of the flesh. But temptation from the world or from the enemy is from an extrinsic principle; hence the act does not belong to the one tempted, but only the undergoing of it. For this reason there is no sin in such temptation except through delight or consent, for then the one tempted begins to cooperate with the tempter. Moreover, according to Thomas, the devil can make impressions on the imaginative power in two ways: by presenting some sensible things outwardly, and by disturbing and altering the imaginative power itself within. Therefore he is said to tempt us according to the mode in which he makes impressions on us. Yet this impression has not the character of sin, since it is not in the appetite but only in the apprehension; but it does tend to sin, as far as the intention of the tempter goes. This too is to be weighed, that, as Thomas adds, a movement of the concupiscible power can arise in us in two ways. First, from the quality of the organ, as when the body is heated a movement of lust arises without any imagination; and this movement is purely natural, not having the character of sin. And this movement the devil can cause in us by his power, unless he is restrained by divine power. Secondly, from the apprehension of something delightful. And on that side the appetite has some freedom in man, in so far as it can obey the command of reason; and so there can be sin in the concupiscible power. But this movement the devil cannot extort.

paras.t: Hæc dicta sint pro pleno hujus loci intellectu, quia materia practica est et salubris. At vero, sicut nonnulli errarunt dicendo interiores tentationes ad vitia inclinantes esse a Deo ; sic alii, ut Pelagiani hæretici, errabant dicentes opera meritoria esse a nobis ipsis, ita quod sine gratia posset homo esse virtute præditus, et Deo acceptus, ac vitam promereri æternam. Dicebant enim : A Deo habemus quod sumus, a nobis ipsis quod justi sumus. Contra hos subdit apostolus Jacobus : Omne datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum desursum est, descendens a Patre luminum. Certum est apud philosophos, omne quod circa Deum est, a Deo fluxisse mediate vel immediate, Aristotele protestante, Ab hoc ente omnibus communicatum est esse et vivere ; atque auctore libri de Causis, Omnis causa primaria plus influit quam quæcumque causa secunda. Verumtamen, aliter dicunt sancti theologi virtutes et actiones meritorias esse a Deo, quam philosophi : quia philosophi dixerunt hominem naturali potestate et propria ratione posse virtutes acquirere, et felicitatem mereri. Quod quamvis verum sit aliquo modo de virtutibus naturalibus, politicis, in beatitudine naturali : theologi tamen affirmant hominem (quia ad supernaturalem beatitudinem est creatus) indigere gratia gratum faciente, virtutibusque infusis, supernaturalibus ac theologicis, et insuper actuali motione Spiritus Sancti in omni meritorio actu, ut sic media correspondeant fini. Quamvis itaque per datum optimum, possunt intelligi naturalia dona suprema in intellectualibus creaturis, ut sunt memoria, intellectus, voluntas, in quibus supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis imago relucet in homine ; per donum vero perfectum, dona supernaturalia, gratuita et infusa, ac meritoria opera, quæ omnia immediate descendunt, causantur, dependent a Deo : possunt tamen per datum optimum, intelligi dona supernaturalia et infusa gratiæ gratis datæ, bonis et malis communia, ut sunt gratia prophetiæ, genera linguarum, sermo sapientiæ, sermo scientiæ, etc., de quibus Corinthiis scribit Apostolus ; per dona vero perfecta, dona gratiæ gratum facientis, virtutes infusæ, dona et fructus spiritus, ac beatitudinis viæ. Nihilo minus omnia ista intelligi possunt per data optima : et per dona perfecta, intelligenda erunt dona gloriæ, dona animæ et corporis glorificati, et quidquid ad cœlestis beatitudinis plenitudinem spectat, quæ vere est status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus, de quibus Isaias et Paulus fatentur : Oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se.
paras.en: Let these things be said for the full understanding of this place, for the matter is practical and wholesome. But just as some erred in saying that inward temptations inclining to vices are from God, so others, like the Pelagian heretics, erred in saying that meritorious works are from ourselves, so that without grace a man could be endowed with virtue, acceptable to God, and merit eternal life. For they said: From God we have that we are; from ourselves, that we are just. Against these the apostle James adds: [[1:17|Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights|Omne datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum desursum est, descendens a Patre luminum]]. It is certain among the philosophers that everything that is around God has flowed from God, mediately or immediately, as Aristotle declares: From this being, being and living are communicated to all things; and as the author of the book On Causes says: Every primary cause flows in more than any secondary cause. Yet the holy theologians say otherwise than the philosophers that the virtues and meritorious actions are from God: for the philosophers said that man by natural power and his own reason can acquire the virtues and merit happiness. And though this is in some way true of the natural, political virtues, in respect of natural beatitude, the theologians affirm that man (because he was created for supernatural beatitude) needs sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God], and infused, supernatural and theological virtues, and besides the actual motion of the Holy Ghost in every meritorious act, so that the means may correspond to the end. Although, then, by *best gift* [Latin *datum*] may be understood the highest natural gifts in intellectual creatures, such as memory, understanding and will, in which the image of the supremely glorious Trinity shines forth in man; and by *perfect gift* [Latin *donum*] the supernatural, gratuitous and infused gifts, and meritorious works, all of which descend, are caused and depend immediately on God: yet by *best gift* may be understood the supernatural infused gifts of gratuitous grace [*gratia gratis data*, graces given for others' good], common to good and bad, such as the grace of prophecy, kinds of tongues, the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, etc., of which the Apostle writes to the Corinthians[[1 Cor 12:8||]]; and by *perfect gifts* the gifts of sanctifying grace, the infused virtues, the gifts and fruits of the Spirit, and the beatitudes of the way. Nonetheless all these can be understood by the best gifts; and then by the perfect gifts will be understood the gifts of glory, the endowments of the glorified soul and body, and whatever belongs to the fullness of heavenly beatitude, which truly is a state made perfect by the gathering of all goods, of which Isaias[[Is 64:4||]] and Paul declare: [[1 Cor 2:9|eye hath not seen, nor ear heard: neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him|Oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se]].

paras.t: Porro per Patrem luminum, intelligi potest Pater æternus, a quo lumen sibi coæternum, unigenitus Filius ejus, invariabiliter oritur. A Patre quoque et Filio, tanquam ab uno fonte ac æternali principio, oritur Spiritus Sanctus Patri Filioque æqualis. Nec tamen Filius et Spiritus Sanctus sunt duo lumina : imo tota superdignissima, superessentialis et incomprehensibilis Trinitas, unum est lumen, sicut et una essentia. Ideo Pater æternus dicitur Pater luminum, quippe qui sit increati luminis et omnis lucis creatæ principium. Aptius tamen hoc loco per Patrem luminum intelligitur Deus Trinitas, universorum creator, cui quotidie dicimus : Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. De quo in Deuteronomio habetur : Nonne ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te, et fecit et creavit te? De quo et Isaias : Et nunc, pater noster es tu, nos vero lutum. Cui et Eliu locutus est : Pater mi, ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis, qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam. Denique huic verbo apostoli Jacobi consonat illud Joannis, Non potest homo accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cœlo; et quod loquitur Paulus, Quid habes quod non accepisti?
paras.en: Further, by the Father of lights may be understood the eternal Father, from whom the light coeternal with Him, His only-begotten Son, unchangeably springs. From the Father and the Son too, as from one fount and eternal principle, proceeds the Holy Ghost, equal to the Father and the Son. Yet the Son and the Holy Ghost are not two lights; nay, the whole supremely worthy, superessential and incomprehensible Trinity is one light, as also one essence. Therefore the eternal Father is called the Father of lights, as being the principle of the uncreated light and of all created light. More fittingly, however, by the Father of lights in this place is understood God the Trinity, Creator of all things, to whom we say daily: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster, qui es in cœlis]]. Of whom it is said in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:6|Is not he thy father, that hath possessed thee, and made thee, and created thee?|Nonne ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te, et fecit et creavit te?]]? Of whom Isaias also says: And now, [[Is 64:8|thou art our father, and we are clay|pater noster es tu, nos vero lutum]]. To whom also Eliu spoke: My father, [[Job 34:36|cease not from the man of iniquity|ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis]], [[Job 34:37|Because he addeth blasphemy upon his sins|qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam]]. Finally, with this word of the apostle James agrees that of John: [[John 3:27|A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven|Non potest homo accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cœlo]]; and what Paul says: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]?

paras.t: Apud quem non est transmutatio : quia omnimoda incommutabilitas, quæ est plena immortalitas, competit Deo, quum sit purus actus, in quo nec est potentia limitans, nec differentia contrahens, neque materia usquam coarctans, ut in Metaphysica sua sapientissime docet Philosophus. Et Proclus Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica subtilissime probat hoc. Unde in Malachia contestatur : Ego Dominus, et non mutor. Quod Balaam quoque adstruit, loquens : Non est Deus quasi homo, ut mentiatur ; nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur. Et sicut contingentia, variabilia, corporalia invariabiliter intelligit, ita et immutabilis permanens, omnia operatur, sicut ait Boetius : O qui perpetua mundum ratione gubernas, . . . tempus ab ævo Ire jubes, stabilisque manens, das cuncta moveri. Quod et primo Timæi disseruit Plato. Propter quod asserit Veritas : Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Nec vicissitudinis obumbratio, id est alicujus successionis obscuratio : quia in supersimplicissimo Deo sunt penitus idem, essentia, potestas et actio, seu esse, posse et agere. Et ipse unico, simplicissimo, et æterno actu intelligit, et vult ac disponit universa et singula in se ipso. Unde et ejus mensura est æternitas, quæ est interminabilis vitæ tota simul perfecta possessio.
paras.en: [[1:17|with whom there is no change|Apud quem non est transmutatio]]: for complete unchangeableness, which is full immortality, belongs to God, since He is pure act, in whom there is neither limiting potency, nor contracting difference, nor matter confining anywhere, as the Philosopher most wisely teaches in his Metaphysics. And Proclus the Platonist proves this most subtly in his Elements of Theology. Hence it is declared in Malachias: [[Mal 3:6|I am the Lord, and I change not|Ego Dominus, et non mutor]]. Which Balaam also affirms, saying: [[Num 23:19|God is not a man, that he should lie, nor is the son of man, that he should be changed|Non est Deus quasi homo, ut mentiatur ; nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur]]. And as He understands contingent, variable, bodily things unchangeably, so also, remaining immutable, He works all things, as Boethius says: O Thou who governest the world by everlasting reason, … who biddest time go forth from eternity, and, abiding unmoved, givest motion to all things. Which Plato also discussed in the first book of the Timæus. Therefore the Truth asserts: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. [[1:17|nor shadow of alteration|Nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]], that is, the darkening of any succession: for in the supremely simple God essence, power and action, or being, being able and acting, are wholly the same. And He by one most simple and eternal act understands, wills and disposes all things and each in Himself. Hence His measure is eternity, which is the perfect possession, all at once, of interminable life.

paras.t: Voluntarie genuit nos verbo veritatis. Hoc multipliciter potest exponi : Primo, quod Pater per Unigenitum suum nos condidit, juxta illud Joannis, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Unde Apostolus : Ex ipso, inquit, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia. Generatio autem in Scripturis interdum pro creatione accipitur, ut ubi legitur : Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ in die quando creatæ sunt. Secundo, quod Deus Trinitas spiritualiter regeneravit nos, id est, ab erroribus et peccatis ad esse gratiæ ac virtutum deduxit nos verbo veritatis, hoc est per doctrinam evangelicæ prædicationis : quod fecit per Christi discipulos, quemadmodum Paulus scribit Corinthiis, In Christo per Evangelium ego vos genui; atque ad Galatas, Filioli (ait) mei, quos iterum parturio, donec formetur Christus in vobis. Tertio, quod Deus per sacramentum Baptismi sub debita forma verborum spiritualiter nos regeneravit. Accedit siquidem verbum ad elementum, et fit sacramentum. Hinc Christus : Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Ad Ephesios quoque ait Apostolus : Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, mundans illam lavacro aquæ in verbo vitæ. Denique quum sacramentum Pœnitentiæ sit secunda post naufragium tabula regenerans, ita fit etiam quotidie in Pœnitentiæ sacramento. Et quoniam Christus Verbum Patris incarnatum instituit sacramenta evangelicæ legis, intelligi potest, quod Pater Verbo veritatis, id est per Verbum suum æternum et increatum, quod est veritas ipsa, præfatis nos modis regeneravit.
paras.en: [[1:18|For of his own will hath he begotten us by the word of truth|Voluntarie genuit nos verbo veritatis]]. This can be expounded in many ways. First, that the Father made us through His Only-begotten, according to that of John: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:36|For of him, and by him, and in him, are all things|Ex ipso, inquit, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia]]. Now generation in the Scriptures is sometimes taken for creation, as where we read: [[Gen 2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth, when they were created|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ in die quando creatæ sunt]]. Secondly, that God the Trinity has spiritually regenerated us, that is, has brought us from errors and sins to the being of grace and virtues by the word of truth, that is, by the teaching of gospel preaching; which He did through the disciples of Christ, as Paul writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 4:15|in Christ Jesus, by the gospel, I have begotten you|In Christo per Evangelium ego vos genui]]; and to the Galatians: [[Gal 4:19|My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you|Filioli … mei … formetur Christus in vobis]]. Thirdly, that God has spiritually regenerated us through the sacrament of Baptism under the due form of words. For the word comes to the element and it becomes a sacrament. Hence Christ says: [[John 3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei]]. To the Ephesians also the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:25|Christ also loved the church|Christus dilexit Ecclesiam]], [[Eph 5:26|cleansing it by the laver of water in the word of life|mundans illam lavacro aquæ in verbo vitæ]]. Further, since the sacrament of Penance is the second plank after shipwreck, regenerating us, so this is also done daily in the sacrament of Penance. And since Christ, the incarnate Word of the Father, instituted the sacraments of the gospel law, it can be understood that the Father has regenerated us in the aforesaid ways by the Word of truth, that is, through His eternal and uncreated Word, which is truth itself.

paras.t: Hæc autem fecit Deus voluntarie, non coacte aut necessitate naturæ, sicut per Osee testatur : Diligam eos spontanee. Et teste Apostolo, Deus operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Per quod refutatur error quorumdam philosophorum et hæreticorum, qui asseruerunt processionem creaturarum a Creatore esse naturalem emicationem ac emanationem, non liberam. Contra quos etiam Plato ait in primo Timæi : Optimus erat Deus. Porro ab optimo longe relegata est omnis invidia. Voluit ergo Deus omnia suæ bonitatis aut beatitudinis esse participia : quam quidem Dei voluntatem si quis rerum principium dixerit, recte eum putare consentiam.
paras.en: Now God did these things of His own will, not under compulsion or by necessity of nature, as He testifies through Osee: [[Osee 14:5|I will love them freely|Diligam eos spontanee]]. And, as the Apostle witnesses, God [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ]]. By this is refuted the error of certain philosophers and heretics who asserted that the procession of creatures from the Creator is a natural outflashing and emanation, not a free one. Against whom Plato too says in the first book of the Timæus: God was most good; and from the most good all envy is far banished. God therefore willed all things to be sharers of His goodness or beatitude; and if anyone should call this will of God the principle of things, I will agree that he judges rightly.

paras.t: Sic ergo nos genuit, ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus, id est, inter corporales ipsius creaturas habeamus primatum : quibus non solum per dona gratiæ, imo et per dona naturæ præferimur. Propter quod dixit Deus : Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram ; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ. Moyses quoque : Solem et lunam et omnia astra creavit Deus in ministerium cunctis gentibus. Porro, per dona gratiæ Christiani ceteris omnibus mundi hominibus incomparabiliter præferuntur, quum sint adoptivi filii Dei, et ejus heredes, et Christi membra ac coheredes. Et ipsi soli sunt in statu salutis, ceteri omnes in statu damnationis, suntque membra, filii ac ministri diaboli. Præterea, quod loquitur Moyses de excellentia populi Israelitici ad Deum tunc pertinentis, dicendo, Non est alia natio tam grandis ; itemque, Quæ est gens una in terra sic inclyta, etc. ? nunc multo præclarius dici potest de populo veraciter christiano, de quo princeps Apostolorum testatur : Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis. Sed, proh dolor ! homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, et multi Christianorum gentilibus deterius vivunt. Postremo, pro eo quod hic dicitur, Ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus, alia littera continet : Ut simus primitiæ creaturarum ejus. Primitias namque frugum et animalium jussit lex Domino consecrari, id est optima quæque in frugibus ac animantibus. Ita et Deus verbo veritatis nos genuit, ut inter omnes homines simus optimus populus ejus.
paras.en: So then He begot us, [[1:18|that we might be some beginning of his creature|ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus]], that is, that we might have the primacy among His bodily creatures, above which we are preferred not only by the gifts of grace but also by the gifts of nature. Therefore God said: [[Gen 1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness: and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and the beasts, and the whole earth|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram ; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ]] [Denis has *and every creature* for *the whole earth*]. Moses also says that God created the sun and moon and all the stars for the service of all nations[[Deut 4:19||]]. Further, by the gifts of grace Christians are incomparably preferred to all other men of the world, since they are adopted sons of God, and His heirs, and members and joint heirs of Christ[[Rom 8:17||]]. And they alone are in the state of salvation; all the others are in the state of damnation, and are members, sons and ministers of the devil. Moreover, what Moses says of the excellence of the people of Israel, which then belonged to God, saying: [[Deut 4:7|Neither is there any other nation so great|Non est alia natio tam grandis]]; and again: [[Deut 4:8|what other nation is there so renowned|Quæ est gens una in terra sic inclyta]], etc.? can now be said much more gloriously of the truly Christian people, of whom the prince of the Apostles testifies: [[1 Pet 2:9|you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people|Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis]]. But, alas! [[Ps 48:13|man when he was in honour did not understand|homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit]], and many Christians live worse than the heathen. Lastly, for what is said here, That we might be some beginning of his creature, another reading has: That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures. For the law commanded the firstfruits of crops and of animals to be consecrated to the Lord, that is, all the best among crops and animals. So also God begot us by the word of truth, that among all men we might be His best people.

paras.t: Scitis, fratres mei dilectissimi, id est, notum vobis est, universa quæ scribo esse verissima, quia scitis Apostolos primitias accepisse Spiritus Sancti. Verumtamen non sufficit vobis hoc scire. Ideo subditur : Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum verba salutis. Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud; et, Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Idcirco, ut in Ecclesiastico dicitur. Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam. Tardus autem ad loquendum : quia hoc sapientiæ signum est, eo quod Salomone testante, in multiloquio non desit peccatum. Atque idem alibi : Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum. Et denuo : Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur : Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam.
paras.en: [[1:19|You know, my dearest brethren|Scitis, fratres mei dilectissimi]], that is, it is known to you that all I write is most true, for you know that the Apostles received the firstfruits of the Holy Ghost[[Rom 8:23||]]. But it is not enough for you to know this. Therefore he adds: [[1:19|And let every man be swift to hear|Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum]] the words of salvation. For [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]; and: [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]. Therefore, as is said in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 3:31|a good ear will hear wisdom with all desire|Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam]]. [[1:19|but slow to speak|Tardus autem ad loquendum]]: for this is a sign of wisdom, since, as Solomon testifies, [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|in multiloquio non desit peccatum]]. And the same elsewhere: [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind: a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum]]. And again: [[Prov 29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment|Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 20:8|He that useth many words shall hurt his own soul|Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam]].

paras.t: Verumtamen in omnibus istis necessaria valde est discretio, ut sit homo quantum in se est, velox ad audiendum, et tardus ad loquendum : quod tamen ad juniores ac subditos et indoctos potissimum pertinet. Nihilo minus, causa rationabili exigente, sit homo velox ad loquendum, præsertim qui præest, dum fraterna correptio aut justa correctio sunt delinquentibus impendendæ, dum etiam proximus indiget informatione, aut revocatione a culpa atque periculis quibus appropinquat. Ideo Salomon dixit : Tempus loquendi, et tempus tacendi est. Atque in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Est tacens, qui invenitur sapiens; est autem tacens, non habens sensum loquelæ; et est tacens, sciens tempus aptum. Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabit tempus. Sic et juniores ac subditi et indocti, dum ex ignorantia sibi periculum vident instare, mox seniores, sapientiores et superiores suos debent interrogare, et eos cum omni reverentia ac aviditate audire, juxta illud : In multitudine presbyterorum prudentium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere. Hinc alibi dicitur : Non te prætereat narratio seniorum. Denique, quam salubre est verba salutis audire, tam periculosum est verba audire vana, scurrilia, detractoria et iniqua, quæ mentem maculant audientis, si ea libenter audierit, aut eis consenserit. A talibus ergo verbis avertatur auditus, si fieri potest, atque ad minus ratio ea detestetur. Ideo ait Scriptura : Sepi aures tuas spinis, et noli audire linguam nequam. Propheta quoque locutus est Deo : Narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes, sed non ut lex tua.
paras.en: Yet in all these things discretion is very necessary, so that a man be, as far as in him lies, swift to hear and slow to speak; which nevertheless belongs chiefly to the younger, to subjects and to the unlearned. Nonetheless, when reasonable cause requires, let a man be swift to speak, especially one who is set over others, when fraternal reproof or just correction must be given to wrongdoers, and when one's neighbour needs instruction, or calling back from sin and from the dangers he is approaching. Therefore Solomon said: [[Eccles 3:7|a time to speak|Tempus loquendi, et tempus tacendi est]]. And in Ecclesiasticus it is said: [[Ecclus 20:5|There is one that holdeth his peace, that is found wise|Est tacens, qui invenitur sapiens]]; [[Ecclus 20:6|There is one that holdeth his peace, because he knoweth not what to say: and there is another that holdeth his peace, knowing the proper time.|est autem tacens, non habens sensum loquelæ; et est tacens, sciens tempus aptum]]. [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time.|Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabit tempus]]. So also the younger, subjects and the unlearned, when they see danger threatening them from ignorance, ought at once to ask their elders, the wiser and their superiors, and to hear them with all reverence and eagerness, according to that: [[Ecclus 6:35|Stand in the multitude of ancients that are wise, and join thyself from thy heart to their wisdom|In multitudine presbyterorum prudentium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere]]. Hence it is said elsewhere: [[Ecclus 8:11|Let not the discourse of the ancients escape thee|Non te prætereat narratio seniorum]]. Further, as wholesome as it is to hear the words of salvation, so dangerous is it to hear vain, scurrilous, detracting and wicked words, which stain the mind of the hearer if he hears them willingly or consents to them. From such words, then, let the hearing be turned away, if it can be done, and at least let reason detest them. Therefore Scripture says: [[Ecclus 28:28|Hedge in thy ears with thorns, hear not a wicked tongue|Sepi aures tuas spinis: linguam nequam]]. The Prophet also spoke to God: [[Ps 118:85|The wicked have told me fables: but not as thy law|Narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes, sed non ut lex tua]].

paras.t: Circa hunc locum loquitur Beda : Qui sapientiam diligit, primo postulet eam a Deo, deinde magistrum veritatis humiliter audiat, et inter agendum suam cautissime coerceat linguam. Tutius enim veritas auditur, quam prædicetur. Hinc Pythagorici naturalis scientiæ magisterio præditi, auditores suos per quinquennium jusserunt silere, et postmodum loqui ac docere permiserunt. Unde et Jeremias propheta, bene instructi adolescentis vitam describens, modestiam taciturnitatis inter prima virtutum studia computat : Bonum est, inquiens, viro, quum portaverit jugum ab adolescentia sua ; sedebit solitarius, et tacebit.
paras.en: On this place Bede says: Let him who loves wisdom first ask it of God, then humbly hear the master of truth, and in the meantime most carefully restrain his tongue. For truth is more safely heard than preached. Hence the Pythagoreans, endowed with the mastery of natural science, ordered their hearers to keep silence for five years, and afterwards allowed them to speak and teach. Hence too the prophet Jeremias, describing the life of a well-instructed youth, counts the modesty of silence among the first pursuits of the virtues, saying: [[Lam 3:27|It is good for a man, when he hath borne the yoke from his youth|Bonum est, inquiens, viro, quum portaverit jugum ab adolescentia sua]]; [[Lam 3:28|He shall sit solitary, and hold his peace|sedebit solitarius, et tacebit]].

paras.t: Itaque per prædicta reprehenduntur, qui ad fabulandum, ad docendum, ad prædicandum sunt promptuli, quum nondum in virtutibus exercitati, nondum sufficienter edocti, nondum a vanitatum expurgati vitiis sint. Verumtamen, cui ex officio incumbit docendi aut prædicandi necessitas, studeat se ad exercendum hos actus exhibere idoneum, in virtutibus ac sapientia proficiendo quotidie, et interim quod per se ipsum facere nequit, per alios idoneos faciat.
paras.en: Thus by the foregoing are rebuked those who are quick to chatter, to teach, to preach, when they are not yet exercised in the virtues, not yet sufficiently taught, not yet purged from the vices of vanities. Yet let him on whom the necessity of teaching or preaching falls by office strive to make himself fit to exercise these acts, advancing daily in virtues and wisdom; and meanwhile what he cannot do himself, let him do through other fit persons.

paras.t: Sit quoque omnis homo et tardus ad iram. Ira est appetitus vindictæ propter illatam injuriam. Et ista est duplex : Una, quæ rationem prævenit et excæcat, quæ vocatur ira per vitium, quia ratione non regitur, nec secundum ordinem juris tendit in ultionem. Ad hanc sic tardi esse debemus, ut eam nunquam admittamus : vel si oriri cœperit, statim per rationis censuram mansuetudinisque virtutem frenetur et extinguatur ; vel saltem sic cohibeatur ne per verba aut signa erumpat, neque per inhonestos apparatus pandatur, sicque paulatim suffocetur in semetipsa. Alia est ira per zelum, quæ rationem sequens, sponte assumitur, ut actus virtutis robustius exerceatur. Et ista est bona, quia per eam secundum rationis judicium fit vindicta. Non tamen est passim atque faciliter admittenda, quia et ipsa rationem aliqualiter turbat, secundum Gregorium. Idcirco ad eam tardi esse debemus, et tunc eam assumere quando aliter actus justitiæ tam convenienter exerceri non valet, ut si quis durus incorrigibilisque exsistat. Et hæc ira fuit in Christo, juxta illud : Contristatus est Jesus super cæcitate cordis eorum, circumspiciens eos cum ira. Hinc loquitur Beda : Tardos ad iram nos esse præcepit, ut non ob quaslibet causas, serenitatem nostri cordis ac vultus in austeritatem vertamus ; sed certa exsistente ratione, verbi gratia, si aliter corrigi proximos, maxime eos qui nobis commissi sunt, non posse conspicimus, severitatem verbi aut districtionem judicii erga eos exhibeamus, manente tamen, quantum humana natura patitur, statu nostræ mentis sereno. Sic Phinees, Samuel, Elias et Petrus, tardi fuerunt ad iram, qui tamen peccantes gladio peremerunt aut verbo. Sic et Moyses quum esset vir mitissimus, exivit a Pharaone iratus nimis, comminatus ei pœnam, quam et opere perpetravit ; qui etiam vituli aurei adoratores districte punivit. Hinc teste Gregorio, Ira non debet rationem quasi domina præcedere, sed tanquam ancilla sequi.
paras.en: Let every man also be [[1:19|slow to anger|et tardus ad iram]]. Anger is the desire of vengeance for an injury inflicted. And it is twofold. One kind forestalls reason and blinds it, and is called anger through vice, because it is not ruled by reason and does not tend to vengeance according to the order of right. To this we ought to be so slow as never to admit it; or if it begins to arise, let it at once be bridled and extinguished by the censure of reason and the virtue of meekness; or at least let it be so restrained that it does not break out in words or signs, nor show itself by unseemly displays, and so little by little be stifled in itself. The other is anger through zeal, which, following reason, is taken up deliberately, so that an act of virtue may be exercised more vigorously. And this is good, because through it vengeance is done according to the judgment of reason. Yet it is not to be admitted everywhere and easily, because it too troubles reason somewhat, according to Gregory. Therefore we ought to be slow to it, and take it up only when an act of justice cannot otherwise be so fittingly exercised, as when someone proves hard and incorrigible. And this anger was in Christ, according to that: [[Mark 3:5|looking round about on them with anger, being grieved for the blindness of their hearts|Contristatus est Jesus super cæcitate cordis eorum, circumspiciens eos cum ira]]. Hence Bede says: He commanded us to be slow to anger, so that we do not for any cause whatever turn the serenity of our heart and countenance into severity; but when there is a sure reason, for example, if we see that our neighbours, especially those committed to us, cannot otherwise be corrected, we may show them severity of word or strictness of judgment, while the state of our mind nevertheless remains serene, as far as human nature allows. Thus Phinees[[Num 25:7||]], Samuel[[1 Kings 15:33||]], Elias[[3 Kings 18:40||]] and Peter[[Matt 26:51||]][[Acts 5:1||]] were slow to anger, who yet slew sinners with the sword or with a word. So too Moses, though he was the mildest of men[[Num 12:3||]], went out from Pharao exceeding angry[[Ex 11:8||]] [the margin gives Exod. xi, 9; the words are at 11:8], threatening him with a punishment which he also carried out in deed; who also strictly punished the worshippers of the golden calf[[Ex 32:27||]]. Hence, as Gregory witnesses, anger ought not to go before reason like a mistress, but follow it like a handmaid.

paras.t: Porro ira per vitium, dupliciter fit mortalis : primo, propter commotionis immoderantiam nimis immoderatam, rationemque penitus offuscantem ; secundo, propter ultionis excessum, ut si quis pro illata sibi injuria, exercere cupiat sive exerceat ultionem tam grandem ut directe contrarietur justitiæ. Denique iram Scriptura valde vituperat et condemnat, stultitiam vocat, et iracundum stulto assimilat. Ait namque Salvator : Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio. Salomon quoque : Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere ? Et iterum Salomon loquitur : Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit. Et Job : Virum stultum interficit iracundia. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Quid iracundo furor suus confert, quem sævissimis exagitat stimulis ? Sicque ab omni mentis consilio alienat, ut dum irascitur, insanire credatur. Idcirco abbas Agathon dixit : Iracundus homo, etiam si mortuos suscitet, Deo non placet. Imo quam nociva sit ira, pandit Gregorius, dicens : Per iram justitia relinquitur, gratia vitæ socialis amittitur, mansuetudo aufertur, lux veritatis repellitur. Hinc Jacobus subdit :
paras.en: Further, anger through vice becomes mortal in two ways: first, through an excessive immoderation of agitation, wholly darkening reason; secondly, through excess of vengeance, as when someone, for an injury done to him, desires to take or takes a vengeance so great that it is directly contrary to justice. Moreover, Scripture greatly reproves and condemns anger, calls it folly, and likens the angry man to a fool. For the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:22|whosoever is angry with his brother, shall be in danger of the judgment|Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio]]. Solomon also: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere]]? And again Solomon says: [[Eccles 7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit]]. And Job: [[Job 5:2|Anger indeed killeth the foolish|Virum stultum interficit iracundia]]. Hence Jerome says: What does his fury profit the angry man, whom it drives on with the cruellest goads? And it so estranges him from all counsel of mind that while he is angry he is thought to be mad. Therefore abbot Agathon said: An angry man, even if he raises the dead, does not please God. Indeed, how harmful anger is Gregory shows, saying: Through anger justice is forsaken, the grace of social life is lost, meekness is taken away, the light of truth is driven back. Hence James adds:

paras.t: Ira enim viri, justitiam Dei non operatur. Sobrie loquitur sanctus ille Apostolus: siquidem minus dicitur, et majus significatur.
